demo:
def greet(name):
    print("Hello,", name)

# "Perth" is the argument
greet("Perth")
note: The value is the argument; the name it arrives under inside the function is the [[parameter]].
short: The actual value you hand to a function when you call it.

demo:
def area(width, height):
    # width and height are the parameters
    return width * height

print(area(3, 4))
note: A parameter is a name waiting for a value; an [[argument]] is the value that turns up.
short: The name a function gives to a value it is handed, written in its def line.

demo:
def double(n):
    return n * 2

result = double(21)
print(result)
print(double(5) + 1)
note: Returning is not printing. A function that prints shows you something; a function that returns gives you something you can use.
short: Hands a value back to whoever called the function, and stops the function there.

demo:
def shows(n):
    print(n * 2)

value = shows(21)
print("the call was worth:", value)
note: A function that prints instead of returning gives the caller nothing: the call is worth None.
short: Writes something on the screen for a person to read.

demo:
def nothing():
    pass

print(nothing())
print(None is None)
note: A function with no return statement hands back None, which is why printing its result shows None.
short: Python's word for "no value at all".

demo:
prices = [3, 5]
prices.append(7)
print(prices)
note: Changing a mutable value changes it for every name pointing at it — see [[aliasing]].
short: Able to be changed after it is made. Lists, dictionaries and sets are mutable.

demo:
name = "perth"
upper = name.upper()
print(name)
print(upper)
note: Operations that look like changes build a new value instead and leave the old one alone.
short: Cannot be changed once made. Strings, numbers and tuples are immutable.

demo:
a = [1, 2]
b = a
b.append(3)
print(a)
print(a is b)
note: Assigning a list to a second name does not copy it. Use list(...) or a slice to get a copy.
short: Two names pointing at the same value, so a change through one shows through the other.

demo:
days = ["Mon", "Tue", "Wed"]
print(days[0])
print(days[-1])
print(len(days))
note: The last item is at index len(x) - 1, which is why len(x) itself is out of range.
short: The position of an item in a list or string, counting from 0.

demo:
word = "Fremantle"
print(word[0:4])
print(word[:3])
print(word[-3:])
note: The stop position is not included, so x[0:2] gives two items.
short: A piece of a list or string, written x[start:stop].

demo:
point = (3, 4)
x, y = point
print(x, y)
print(len(point))
note: Like a list but immutable, which makes it safe to use as a dictionary key.
short: A fixed sequence of values, written with round brackets: (1, 2).

note: Asking for a key that is not there raises KeyError; .get() returns None instead.
short: The thing you look something up by in a dictionary.

note: Looping over a dictionary gives you its keys, not its values.
short: To go through something one item at a time, which is what a for loop does.

demo:
total = 0
for n in [2, 4, 6]:
    total = total + n
print(total)
note: It has to be created before the loop starts, or the first pass has nothing to add to.
short: A variable you set up before a loop and add to inside it.

demo:
print(2 + 2)
print("ab" * 3)
print(5 > 3)
short: A piece of code that produces a value: 2 + 2, name.upper(), x > 3.

note: An expression produces a value; a statement does something.
short: A complete instruction: an assignment, an if, a loop, a return.

demo:
print(3 > 5)
print(bool(0), bool(""), bool([]))
print(bool("no"), bool([0]))
note: Python also treats 0, "" and [] as false when it needs a yes or no, which is what "falsy" means.
short: A value that is either True or False.

demo:
print(0.1 + 0.2)
print(7 / 2)
print(round(2.675, 2))
note: Floats are stored in binary, so some sums come out a hair off: 0.1 + 0.2 is not exactly 0.3.
short: A number with a decimal point, like 3.5.

demo:
print(7 / 2)
print(7 // 2)
print(-7 // 2)
note: Dividing with / always gives a float; // keeps it whole and rounds down.
short: A whole number, with no decimal point.

demo:
first = "Swan"
print(first + " River")
print(first + str(2))
note: Both sides have to be strings: adding a number raises TypeError unless you convert it first.
short: To join two strings end to end with +.

demo:
name = "  perth  "
print(name.strip().title())
print("a,b".split(","))
note: A method acts on the thing before the dot, which is why it needs no argument for it.
short: A function that belongs to a value, called with a dot: name.upper().
A named block of code you can run whenever you want, by calling it.

demo:
def f():
    inside = 1
    print("inside sees:", inside)

f()
print("outside sees:", "inside" in dir())
note: That is why a variable made in a function vanishes when the function ends.
short: Where a name can be seen. A name made inside a function is only visible inside it.

note: Read it from the bottom: the last line names the error, and the line above it is usually your code.
short: The report Python prints when something goes wrong, listing where it happened.

note: try/except lets you catch one and decide what to do instead of stopping.
short: Python's way of stopping when it cannot carry on, like dividing by zero.

note: A SyntaxError means Python could not read the code at all, so nothing ran — not even the lines above it.
short: The grammar of the language: where the colons, brackets and indents go.

note: Four spaces per level is the convention. Mixing tabs and spaces is a common cause of errors.
short: The spaces at the start of a line, which is how Python knows what is inside what.

note: Without one the calls never stop, and Python gives up with RecursionError.
short: The case a recursive function answers directly, without calling itself again.

note: Every recursive function needs a [[base-case]] or it never stops.
short: A function that calls itself on a smaller version of the same problem.

note: A project brief that fixes a signature means calling it that exact way, with that many parameters.
short: The def line of a function: its name and the parameters it takes.
A value written directly in the code: 42, "hello", [1, 2].
A value an operator works on. In 2 + 3, the operands are 2 and 3.

note: A nested loop runs its whole inner loop for every single pass of the outer one.
short: One thing inside another: a loop inside a loop, or a list inside a list.
